raw_comment:
I noticed that the Gulf of Mexico has heated up quite a lot since February and is now going down. I assume a lot of the heat is due to just the seasons changing. But when you compare the heat to the average temperature per year you can tell the heat is a lot more than normal at some points (Especially August through October). The warm weather has most likely caused some factures of the hurricanes and helped them form. 
I wonder if there are other factors that have caused the heat to rise up so much. 
I feel this could effect more places in the future if other places happen to have effects as major as these. It could cause lots of more hurricanes in other places demolishing and hurting towns or people. 
"Could changing of temperature lead to something greater?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that around May of every single year, the heat content in the Gulf of Mexico rises drastically, and continues to rise until approx. September, when it reaches its peak. It then continues to decrease until the next year when it will repeat its cycle again. This means it moves in a cyclic manner.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if this aggressive influx of heat has anything to do with the intensity of the recent hurricanes that have blown through areas along the Gulf of Mexico. I believe it does. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
Many of the people in my community have family and relatives in Florida, which is oddly very common in New York, who had just been heavily hit by Hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene. If this trend continues to happen, and my hypothesis of the heat and hurricane correlation is correct, this may force them to suffer more.

Catchy Headline: 
"The Waves of Heat Rolling Through The Gulf"

:)

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I noticed that the ocean heat content per square centimeter drastically increased from late April to early October. The largest difference is from May to June, and the peak seems to be in September. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder if global warming would have a significant impact on ocean heat content changes, as the average peak from 2010-2023 was around 70 kJ/cm^2, but on October 7, 2024, the peak was higher than 80. Is it possible to bring down the ocean heat content, and are there going to be serious negative impacts if this trend continues?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because I live in the Bay Area, which is very close to the Pacific Ocean. The weather here is significantly impacted by the ocean, which often brings a cooler climate to help combat the heat. However, if the trend of increasing ocean heat content continues, the cool layer that the ocean brings would have a lesser of an impact, and temperatures would increase each year. There is already evidence of this, as there were heat waves lasting till the first week of October, which was the same time as the peak of ocean heat.  
Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Heating Up Hurricanes: How the Rising Ocean Heat Content is Creating Deadlier Hurricanes.

raw_comment: I noticed in the graph that the energy in the ocean increased as the summer came along. I wonder why the people who made the graph used kilojoules over any other type of measurement, kilojoules are used to measure the energy in food and drinks. Using just normal temperature would have been a bit better. Many people think that the higher amounts of energy in the water is caused by global warming, but if we were to look at the other higher years, they would all be La Nina years, which is part of the 4-year El Nino cycle in weather. In La Nina years, there is more energy in and near the equator, above and below the water, which causes more hurricanes. La Nina years always follow El Nino years, which are the calmest out of all of the years.

raw_comment:
I notice that the ocean heat content rises to above 20 kJ/cm^2 during the” Hurricane season” and stays below 20 kJ/cm^2 outside of the “Hurricane season”. This means that Hurricanes typically form over warmer waters found between June and November due to the summer climate in the Gulf of Mexico.

I wonder what causes the lack of readings between June - July and September-October in certain past years.

As we can see in the graph, every year, the warmth in the Gulf of Mexico gets higher with 2024’s ocean heat content being amongst the highest recorded. This graph is one of many available examples of the effect of global warming on our climate’s behaviors. Our community is also impacted by the global phenomena through wildfires, droughts, and weather pattern inconsistencies. Because of all these issues, we should look at this graph to see and raise awareness of the intense effects of global warming and climate change.

A catchy title for this graph may be
"Hotter Heat Waves and Windier Hurricanes: Tracking the Heat Surge in the Gulf of Mexico, the Birthplace of Tropical Storms."

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice how the gray lines show us the average ocean heat content from the years 2013 to 20-23. The gray lines increased mostly from June and dropped low to the end of November. I notice the red line labeled “Oct. 7 2024” which differs from the average gray line. The red one goes way above the average in June and slowly goes back to normal, but then takes a huge jump in kilojoules from August to October. These lines are not lines at all, they are shaky lines drawn throughout all the averages taken making the graph look very messy and scribbly. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder if climate change has something to do with this extreme jump in ocean heat content, or this was naturally occurring. I wonder if it could have been a mix of both, because climate change has really affected our environment, but hurricanes do occur naturally. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

Hurricane Milton heavily affected Florida and I have family there. They sent us many pictures and videos of the flooding going on and how scary it was for everyone. This happened in our country and I think it’s really important we are aware of what is going on. If these hurricanes were in any way caused due to climate change, I think this really sends a message to our communities to put our heads together and preserve the earth before it is too late to do so.

raw_comment:
1.	What do you notice?
I notice that the red line showing the ocean heat content for 2024, is much higher than the average from 2013 to 2023. It peaked around July and October, reaching a heat content of over 80 kilojoules per square centimeter. The average heat content in the Gulf of Mexico over the past decade rarely reached that high.
	2.	What do you wonder?
I wonder what caused such a big increase in ocean heat this year. Is it linked to climate change or are there specific events like hurricanes that contributed? I also wonder what impact this higher ocean heat might have on weather patterns, marine life, and coastal communities.
	3.	How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because higher ocean temperatures can lead to more intense hurricanes, which could affect coastal areas. If we live near the Gulf of Mexico, warmer waters could increase the likelihood of stronger storms, affecting people’s homes, safety, and the environment.
	4.	Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Gulf of Mexico Heat Soars 2024’s Ocean Temperatures Break Record Levels

raw_comment: Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Multiple Hurricanes from Excess Ocean Heat: Concern for Climate Skyrockets” by Abhiram of California; “We Might Be in Hot Water: The Gulf of Mexico Is Cooking Severe Storms!” by Sadhana of Santa Clara High School; “Intensifying Heat in the Gulf of Mexico Powers Strong Hurricanes” by Giovana of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Convent Station, N.J.; three headlines from Perth Amboy High School in N.J. -- "Rising Gulf Heat Fuels Mega Hurricanes!" by Gerely, “Gulf of Mexico Heatwave: Nature’s Warning Signal for Coastal Havoc” by Esmeily and “Scorching Gulf Waters in 2024 Ignite Record-Breaking Hurricanes!” by Jayden and three headlines from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich. -- “The Gulf of Mexico Is Warming Up: Major Hurricanes Seen as a Result” by Finnegan, “Heat Waves: How Has Warmth in the Gulf of Mexico Contributed to Milton and Helene?” by Avonlea and "World's Worst Hot Tub. The Gulf of Mexico's Unusual Year." by Cade.

raw_comment:
1. From mid-August to June and again from late August to October, the highlighted line shows this year’s heat content in the Gulf of Mexico, deviating from the 10-year average. In the past decade, readings mostly stayed within ±10 kJ/cm² of the average. However, this year’s peaks hit a maximum deviation of about 15 kJ/cm² twice, showing the increasing variability and overall rise in heat content in the Gulf. This increased warmth provides more energy for storms, which have been stronger and more frequent recently.

2. A question could be whether the 2013 data shows the lowest readings, with the next years showing a gradual increase in heat content. If so, this would confirm a consistent warming trend in the Gulf of Mexico, driven by rising greenhouse gas emissions. This trend would suggest that the Gulf will continue to warm, creating more powerful hurricanes. If not, we may need to look at more Gulf heat content data from the past.

3. The rising heat in the Gulf also contributes to more frequent and intense hurricanes that affect the southern U.S., leading to widespread damage and displacement. While I live on the West Coast and am not directly affected, there is still an impact on taxpayers, as funds are needed for emergency relief and rebuilding efforts. Additionally, violent storms pose a hazard to shipping and oil tankers which lead to environmental contamination from spills.

4.“Gulf of Mexico Heat Hits Record Highs in 2024, Ocean Temps Soar Past Decade Average”

raw_comment:
I noticed while analyzing that the information recorded is the temperatures of the Gulf of Mexico throughout the years. Each of the gray lines represented on the graph shows the data of a year between 2013 and 2023. However, the graph also provides a black dotted which represented the found average for the data the gray lines provide. The red line illustrates the information from 2024, which begins to build in June (something that stays consistent throughout all the years). In September of this year, the line reaches higher than 80 kJ/cm^2 - this is the first time that the graph has been significantly higher than this mark. It spikes once more in October, presumably because of the recent Hurricanes. 
I wonder why the red line depicted has gaps within it. For instance, in the beginning of February as well as June. I also wonder what happened in September that caused the graph to spike so high. 
This relates to my community because temperatures of the oceans have only increased as well as the level. This is a direct effect of climate change which affects the entire world. It is hurting sea life and poses many questions for the world. Furthermore, where I live there has been disastrous hurricanes in the past which have had a plethora of effects on my community. 
Rise and Fall: Temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico

raw_comment:
I noticed that the ocean heat content in the Gulf of Mexico for 2024 is much warmer than the average over the past ten years. I also set ocean heat content records for June, August, September, and October. Additionally, the description also says that ocean heat content measures how much thermal energy is stored per unit volume of water, making it a measurement of water warmth. 
Something else I noticed is how each year’s temperature graphs were evenly spaced apart, possibly indicating steady growth, but the gap between this year's graph and the previous highest ocean heat content was immense and oversized. 

I wonder if this increase in ocean heat content is related to the two hurricanes that happened recently, Hurricane Milton in October and Hurricane Helene in September. This is because Hurricanes need warm water to form and grow, specifically above 26 degrees Celsius. 

This relates to my community because rising ocean heat content may contribute to more widespread hurricanes and tropical storms. The reason hurricanes rarely strike California is that the waters around California are too cold to form, grow, and sustain hurricanes enough to reach landfall. However, the drastic increases in ocean temperatures as observed in the graph have the potential to change this. Once ocean temperatures are above 26 C on the West Coast, tropical storms and hurricanes will have the potential to form, possibly devastating communities along the California coast, including my community.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the graph always peaks between August and October. After October, the graph dramatically slopes off and stays that way for months, until about June when it starts to heat up again. This trend is consistent throughout the years, but each year, more heat accumulates in the Gulf of Mexico. 2024 is a bit of an outlier, peaking higher than any year previously and being 20 kJ/cm^2 higher than the decade average.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how much of an impact climate change can have on this. Ocean warming and acidification have been an increasingly worrying problem in the past years due to fossil fuel emission and other factors. I’m curious as to how much this affects this specific case, and how the severity and frequency of ocean storms will increase alongside the temperature of the Gulf.

How does it relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because as a coastal state, we live under an hour away from the ocean. Although we don’t live too close to the Gulf of Mexico specifically, this trend may be happening in the Pacific ocean as well, and if it is, then we’re in for a world of terror. The rising temperature in all large bodies of water can cause tidal waves and monsoons, causing large-scale evacuation measures, which can turn people’s lives upside down.

raw_comment:
Rising Water Temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico Increasing Hurricane Formation Frequency

I notice the graph seems to follow a bell-curve-like pattern, it steadily increases and decreases throughout the year, peaking in mid-August and reaching its lowest in mid-February. Furthermore, throughout the years, the Gulf has consistently reached high temperatures, sooner, than the year before. 

I wonder how much the warmer oceans affect the formation of new hurricanes and their category. I am also curious about how much the high temperatures affected hurricanes Helene and Milton. As ocean warming continues, sea life is increasingly disturbed, which plants and animals have been negatively affected by the rising temperatures, and which ones have benefitted? Looking at the graph, it is clear to see that temperatures rise from year to year, however, I am curious as to the rate of change in temperatures from year to year.

This relates to my community because warmer ocean temperatures mean that hurricanes are more likely. Even though the Bay Area does not directly face hurricanes, the weather effects of hurricanes can still be felt. With more frequent storms, there will be increasing disruptions in the weather and precipitation patterns of the Bay Area. As we saw just recently, the damages from hurricanes are tens of billions of dollars, these damages have ripple effects throughout the economy potentially affecting Bay Area life.

raw_comment:
I notice that the “ocean heat content” starts dramatically rising after April of each year and peaks in around August and September, after which it begins to fall. This year (2024), the ocean heat content has consistently been higher than the average, at one point (near September) being around 15 kJ/cm^2 higher.

I wonder how we can use this graph to predict future patterns and whether the ocean heat content will continue to increase in the coming years due to climate change and global warming. I also want to know how the recent hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico contributed to this pattern.

This relates to my community because we live close to the ocean and might be observing similar patterns that will continue to change with the future of climate change and global warming.

raw_comment:
I notice that the ocean’s heat content in the Gulf of Mexico has followed a trend in the past where its temperature increases from June to August and then decreases from October to December. This year’s data, however, displays a record-high temperature when compared to the past. 

I wonder what the sudden cause of this increase in temperature is. Climate change has been increasing at a significant rate for the last couple of years, but what was it that caused such a high increase this year? What happened differently this year that caused this when compared to last year or the year before?

Temperatures of water bodies, air, and the overall earth have been consistently rising faster than before. This is simply a visual that emphasizes the direness of the situation we are now in. While this graph does not individually indicate what the cause of this increase in temperature is, it is stated that a higher temperature allows storms to strengthen and increase in size. This is important as the number and intensity of storms and hurricanes have been increasing each year, and this could be a significant factor in why. 

The Rise of the Gulf: How Increasing Water Temperatures Could be Affecting the Severity of Storms

raw_comment:
I notice that the graph shows a culmination of different years of ocean heat levels on the same chart. The data uses kilojoules per square centimeter to measure ocean temperatures. Though the data seems random for each individual year, there is a noticeable change in heat levels between the different years. After every year, it seems that the ocean temperatures rise more, and right now we are experiencing higher ocean temperatures than any year since 2013 at the very least. 
I wonder if there is a way to predict what ocean temperatures would be from different years, maybe not for a certain day, week or month, but to compare averages for the whole year. I wonder if there is a common ratio between the ocean temperature throughout the years that can be correlated to human activity. 
This relates to me and my community as these ocean temperatures may represent global temperatures which affect the entire world, leading to more heatwaves in my community specifically, and the loss of wildlife. I also noticed that the article states that warmer waters helped fuel hurricanes, which could drastically affect the states near the Gulf of Mexico, like Florida. 
A catchy headline to capture the main idea of the graph would be, Rising Ocean Temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico and It’s Effect on Weather Patterns.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph follows a similar pattern each year, spiking in kilojoules around mid-August to October, during the peak of hurricane season. Although the energy levels all roughly keep to the same trend, there are still big changes between the data from separate years. The differences are most likely caused by the everlasting issue of global warming, which is proven by the highest line on the chart coming from this year when global temperatures and water levels have been at an all-time high. 
This graph piques my interest because of the disparity between the aspects of it, even though it constantly follows the trendline. I wonder how the lines may advance to the next coming years as the jump from 2023 to 2024 was substantial. I also wonder how it relates to climate change and other worldwide issues of the sort, and how the change or improvement of global warming may affect the energy levels. 
This relates to me and my community because the graph represents global issues and issues in my country that lead to global warming and climate change as a whole. Although the problem is a large one and can not be easily reversed, it is still important to make sure that everyone in all communities is taking steps in the right direction, to avoid the problems that we created in the past, and to make a better future for ourselves and each other. 
A catchy headline for this graph would be “A Mountain of Heat”

raw_comment:
I noticed the ocean’s heat content reached a new high in 2024, largely increasing from that of 2013. I also noticed that heat content begins to rise after April, and starts to fall in October.
I wonder what factors contribute to the rise in ocean heat content, and what caused certain outlying data, such as the drastic drop in August. Are inconsistencies a result of current events in the area, such as increased rainfall? 
This relates to me and my community because warmer oceans increase the risk of heat waves, droughts, and wildfires. The progressive rise in the Gulf of Mexico’s heat content leads to undesirable conditions for the nearby community. The issue of ocean warming is not limited to the Gulf of Mexico, as it is an international issue. It further affects my community as ocean warming contributes to 90% of global warming. 
Unprecedented Heat Surge: Gulf of Mexico Hits New Highs in 2024

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the warmth in the Gulf of Mexico typically peaks after August but then falls around October. It is warmest during the months of June, July, and August where it experiences higher summer temperatures. It then drops very low in the winter months and starts returning to those high temperatures in early spring, around April.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how this correlates with the hurricanes that the area has recently experienced and with climate change. Specifically, how does the temperature intensify hurricanes and storms like Hurricane Helene and Hurricane Milton? Have temperatures increased significantly over decades? How has human activity played a role in impacting these temperatures?

How does this relate to you and your community?
The warming effect seen in the Gulf of Mexico is a trend that is experienced in oceans across the world, including the Pacific coast and it demonstrates the impact human activity has on our global climate. Its effect on our community is shown by strange weather patterns that we have experienced recently, including unusual changes in temperature from previous years.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I noticed that the ocean heat content per square centimeter drastically increased from late April to early October. The largest difference is from May to June, and the peak seems to be in September. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder if global warming would have a significant impact on ocean heat content changes, as the average peak from 2010-2023 was around 70 kJ/cm^2, but on October 7, 2024, the peak was higher than 80. Is it possible to bring down the ocean heat content, and are there going to be serious negative impacts if this trend continues?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because I live in the Bay Area, which is very close to the Pacific Ocean. The weather here is significantly impacted by the ocean, which often brings a cooler climate to help combat the heat. However, if the trend of increasing ocean heat content continues, the cool layer that the ocean brings would have a lesser of an impact, and temperatures would increase each year. There is already evidence of this, as there were heat waves lasting till the first week of October, which was the same time as the peak of ocean heat.  
Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Heating Up Hurricanes: How the Rising Ocean Heat Content is Creating Deadlier Hurricanes.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the graph documents the heat content of the Gulf of Mexico from 2013 through 2024, with kilojoules per square centimeter as the y-axis and the months of the year as the x-axis. I also noticed that the article talked about the hurricanes Milton and Hellene and how they were intensified due to the increased heat content of the water in the Gulf of Mexico. 
2. I wonder why the Gulf of Mexico’s heat content has been slowly but steadily increasing since 2013.  
I also wondered what caused the unfamiliar spike in heat content in 2024 compared to the 2013-2023 interval. 
I wonder if and how ocean heat content data can be utilized to further detect and understand hurricanes to properly decrease their destructive impacts on infrastructure and, more importantly, families. 
3. This relates to me and my community because it is one of the many indicators of climate change that is consistently and inevitably occurring throughout the world. This has caused many detrimental impacts on both ecosystems and human populations including my community. The increase in temperatures has broken down roads, started wild fires that ravaged thousands of acres, and decreased the diversity of wildlife in the area. This serves as a wake-up call both for me and my community to do a better job of protecting our environment and land. 

4. Hurricanes Helene and Milton intensify with the rise in the Gulf of Mexico’s heat content: Is this a wake-up call to stand up to climate change?

raw_comment:
1. This graph is showing the temperature of the Gulf of Mexico. When temperatures are warmer it is easier for strong storms and hurricanes to form. The temperatures are much warmer this year than the average since 2013. The temperatures have been escalating even during the cooler months. There was a large increase between May and June and August and September. 
2. I wonder why the ocean temperature is getting so much warmer in the past couple months. I wonder if the ocean temperature will continue to rise or if it will drop back down again. I wonder if the ocean warms and cools in cycles and this is the warm portion of it or if it is getting warmer all around. 
3. This relates to my community because as the water warms up it is easier for conditions to be right for an intense hurricane. Lots of people are affected by hurricanes each year and warmer Gulf temperatures would only heighten the problem. If we can figure out why the temperature gets warmer maybe scientists can figure out a way to reduce the effects of hurricanes. 
4. A catchy title for this graph could be Caught in Hot Water: Water temperatures rise and so might hurricane intensity.

I notice that the red line which I’m guessing represents the nearest hurricanes, has obtained the highest peak in ocean heat content over the last decade. The graph represents the ocean heat in the Gulf of Mexico over the last decade in kilojoules per square centimeter.
I wonder why in the last decade we see a relatively incremental drop in ocean heat as we head towards the end of the year in November and December.
This shows how much of an effect the hurricanes have impacted certain communities, especially those near the coast because these hurricanes are a precursor to the eventual flooding that inevitably takes place. This also shows the terrible effects of climate change which can completely change the weather patterns all over the world, affecting my community.
Ocean Heat Warmth: Are Hurricanes to Blame for the Steady Rise?

3)This relates to my community because the record-high ocean heat in the Gulf of Mexico increases hurricane risks, disrupts marine life, and may impact local economics through stronger storms and changing weather patterns, affecting both coastal and island communities 

4)Too Hot To Handle: Gulf 2024 Heat Spike

raw_comment:
After looking at the graph, I noticed that it measures the heat of the ocean in the Gulf of Mexico in the past and recent times. Between the months of February through April, the average temperature and the current temperatures are very similar. However, from September through October, the recent temperatures are at their highest. 
This makes me wonder what the factors in the increase of ocean temperatures are. It also makes me wonder about the correlation between previous ocean temperatures and past hurricanes. 
This relates to my community because of the impact the rising heat temperature could have on the environment as well as future weather events. 
A headline for this graph is “Rising Ocean Temperatures and the Threat on Coastal Communities”.

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I notice that the warmth of the Gulf of Mexico has increased by a significant amount.  This drastic change in temperature is seen specifically in the months of April to June, where the temperature spiked above average, and August to October, where the temperatures were greater than double the average.  By further analyzing this information, I notice that both Hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene were said to have intensified over the increasingly warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico.  I wonder if the devastation of these two hurricanes would have been remarkably lower if the waters had been the average temperature or even below average.  I also wonder if this will impact possible future hurricanes during the fall season in the Gulf of Mexico region and area.  I wonder if the spike of warm waters was caused by the harmful effects of global warming in the world.  The warmth of the body of water is affecting natural disasters, which can further damage communities near the Gulf of Mexico and possibly other regions if global warming continues to warm the oceans.  Global warming and its effects impact me and my community because I have seen firsthand warmer winters and summers than I am previously used to.  My community has witnessed warmer seasons due to global warming, and I wonder if I will witness another warmer winter this year.

raw_comment:
This graph represents the oceanic heat in the Gulf of Mexico in kj/cm^2. In the first half of the year (Feb - May), the ocean heat is relatively low, staying constant. However, the heat undergoes a massive spike, which marks the start of summer, and the heat gradually wears until November. The 2024 spike is similar to the average from 2013-23, but it is surpassed by August, peaking at over 80kJ/cm2. The measure from 2013 is much lower and seems to only surpass 60kJ/cm2 by August, and each individual year after is a little bigger, which shows us that the ocean heat in the summer gradually increased year by year. 

I wonder what caused the ocean heat to increase so quickly. What factors led to the acceleration of this trend? I also wonder what factors increase in heat relate to. Will it affect the intensity or the amount of hurricanes and storms that form in the Gulf of Mexico? How will it affect the surrounding ecosystems and marine life? 

As one of the communities living in the Atlantic Coast, environmental factors such as storms and hurricanes are of major concern. This brings on the risk of flooding and property destruction. Furthermore, the formation of cyclones have a devastating effect on marine life, which would negatively impact biodiversity. As such, it is important to keep the trends of climate change in check in order to be better prepared for natural disasters and to preserve the ecosystems.

Ocean Fever: A Dive Into the Warming Waters of the Gulf of Mexico

raw_comment:
This graph displays the rising temperature of the sea in the Gulf of Mexico. It represents the temperature over eleven years (2013-2024). The red line demonstrates the most recent measurement, presumably to inform the reader of the current state of the ocean. I also noticed that the measurements are in kilojoules, an interesting unit. I wonder what the benefit of using kilojoules is over different, more common units. Although I am far from the Gulf of Mexico, its higher temperature can lead to more significant hurricanes that impact more people. As hurricanes increase in frequency and intensity, they may begin to work their way through more of the country.
Catchy title: Can The Gulf of Mexico Take the Heat?

raw_comment:
Headline: Record Gulf Heat Sparks Climate Worries
What do I notice?
The chart measures the ocean heat content in the Gulf of Mexico in kilojoules per square centimeter. The red line representing October 7, 2024, shows significantly higher ocean heat content than the average for 2013-2023, showing unusual warmth.

What do I wonder?
I wonder what the contributing factors are for this extreme warmth in 2024 and how it might affect marine life and communities near the coast.  Could this rise in ocean heat content have an impact on hurricanes or tropical storms in the region?

What do I think is going on in this graph?
The graph suggests a significant increase in ocean heat content in the Gulf of Mexico in 2024 compared to previous years. This could be part of global warming, possibly driven by climate change, which results in higher-than-normal sea temperatures.

How does this relate to you and your community?
Even though I don't live near the Gulf Coast, the rise in ocean temperatures can affect me and my community. Warmer oceans can lead to more extreme weather events like hurricanes, which can badly impact areas near me. Additionally, climate change impacts from rising ocean heat could contribute to higher temperatures, which affects life overall in my community.

What do you notice?
I noticed that the ocean heat in the Gulf of Mexico is the highest this year. It also tends to increase through August and October. It shows the amount of warmth that both Hurricane Milton and Helene used to help them gain the speed for them to be considered hurricanes. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how long it takes for the Gulf of Mexico to get so hot during August through October to create such storms. I wonder if the reason that it gets so hot in the Gulf of Mexico is due to how close it is to the equator. I wonder if the temperatures will just keep increasing for the forseek future.  

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because there is a chance that a hurricane can head our way just like Sandy did in 2012. Also, the majority of the people in my town whose home countries have been affected by hurricanes have been created in the Gulf of Mexico. My home country Dominican Republic has been affected by past hurricanes.

Each line on the graph represents the heat growing each Year and between August and October it shows the peak of the warmth in the Gulf of Mexico. raw_comment:
1. The graph illustrates the rising water temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico. The dashed lines depict the average temperatures throughout the year, while the red line shows the actual temperatures. I observed that the ocean heat content exceeds the average in June and from August to October, indicating an abnormality. However, temperatures appear to be decreasing recently, so we can anticipate a decrease in the upcoming months.
2. I wonder what the cause of abnormally high ocean heat contents is. Is this an effect of Hurricane Milton? Is this another side effect of global warming? Has the average increased over the years? 
3. I may not live near the Gulf of Mexico, but this graph applies to my life because this data may reflect temperature increases in other bodies of water. If ocean heat escalates, at some point in the future, swimming or other water activities may become dangerous in the summer months. I would like to further track this increase to see if this may affect my area. 
4. The Gulf is getting hotter: when a dip in the ocean won't cool you off

1. I notice that the temperatures are following a constant pattern each year, which I found pretty interesting. The hurricane seemed to have some effect on the temperatures, but it did not make a major change the temperature trends. As I was viewing the graph, I notice that the temperatures are rising during June and August, then seem to decrease from October-December.

2. I am curious about how the Gulf is able to heat up quickly in a short period of time. I wonder about the side effects that may have contributed to the rising temperatures in the ocean that occurred very quickly. 

3. This relates to me and my community because hurricanes (especially our most recent ones- Milton and Helene). which are effected by the warm Gulf water temperatures, can lead to major destructions, like power outages, home damages, etc, due to the bad weather conditions and high winds.

4. An uprise in the warmth of the Gulf- leading up to the major hurricanes

raw_comment:
headline: Intensifying Heat in the Gulf of Mexico Powers Strong Hurricanes

The graph measures the warmth of the Gulf of Mexico, specifically—the ocean's heat, over time.  In some parts, I noticed that the red line representing the ocean's heat is higher than the average from 2023-2023. From February to April, the temperatures are pretty average, however May to June there is a significant rise above the average. The ocean heat in October 2024, when the hurricanes are taking place, is much higher compared to previous years (above 80 kj/cm). This makes me wonder what is causing this uprise in heat, one reason potentially being climate change. Also, how does the intense heat create a more powerful hurricane? This graph relates to me and my community because the heat uprising can result in more powerful hurricanes, possibly in my area. Also, more hurricanes in the U.S. means more money is being spent on the clean-up and rebuilding of places hit.

The dotted lines display the average temperance throughout the years and the individual gray lines show each year (2013-2023). The red line shows the temperature increase in 2024, and it stops October 7, 2024, where the temperature is starting to decrease. I also notice that the Gulf is the warmest between August and October. I wonder if the reason the temperature has been high in 2024, compared to the previous years, I know two hurricanes have hit, but hurricanes have hit in previous years and the temperatures haven’t been as high as in 2024. I think that this graph is showing the effects that water temperatures have on hurricanes, and how they can greatly affect the temperature rising in the Gulf of Mexico. This relates to my community because the rise of temperatures due to storms can greatly affect one's health, including my own, and if a hurricane hits New Jersey, the increase of temperature is not great for the environment or the communities health. I notice that there is a graph for the recent hurricanes in our country, and is showing the "ocean heat content" throughout the graph. I notice that there are many lines contributing to the graph. There is a red line, dull gray lines, and a dotted line throughout the graph. I also notice that the ocean is warmer throughout some months during the hurricanes that were occurring. I wonder if there is anything else as extreme as hurricanes that will change the temperature of oceans to such an extreme measure. I also wonder if the ocean heat can predict future hurricanes or other natural disasters. I think, in this graph, that there is a measure of ocean heat content throughout the recent hurricanes, Hurricane Helene and Milton and how it is impacting the Gulf of Mexico. This relates to me and my community by helping us understand how hurricanes are impacting our earth so we can take action if it becomes dangerous.

raw_comment:
1. I’ve noticed that temperatures generally follow a consistent pattern each year, which is interesting. While the hurricane seemed to have some effect, it didn’t drastically change the temperature trends. Typically, temperatures rise during June and August, then decrease from October through December.

2. I’m curious about the hurricane’s impact on water temperatures. There’s a slight increase this year, but I’m unsure if that’s due to the hurricane or just naturally warmer conditions. It would be fascinating to investigate whether the hurricane significantly influenced the water temperature.

3. This issue is personal for me, as many of my friends have family in Florida who were directly affected by the hurricane’s destruction. It’s also a significant concern for all Americans, as natural disasters like this can devastate entire communities.

4. The hurricanes, Milton and Helene, seem to be heating up the ocean.

raw_comment:
The graph shows a clear increase in ocean heat content in the Gulf of Mexico from 2013 to October 2024. I notice that the ocean is warmer between August and October, and this rise in heat seems to coincide with more intense hurricanes, like Milton and Helene. The main red line represents the average heat across all years in the dataset, showing a significant uptick in recent years. I wonder how much this increase in heat has affected the number and strength of hurricanes. The dot at the beginning of October might indicate a return to regular temperatures after the summer heat. For my community, rising ocean temperatures could lead to stronger storms, increasing the risk of flooding and property damage. These changes can also disrupt local ecosystems and affect the food supply, as well as impact the economy through potential job losses and higher insurance costs. Overall, while this graph doesn’t directly impact me as someone who lives in NJ, it highlights how global warming is felt worldwide and its far-reaching effects.

1. On October 7, 2024, I observed an unusual spike in temperature, much higher than typical for that time of year in the Gulf of Mexico. The ocean is generally warm, but on this day, the temperature rose even more noticeably. It started lower earlier in the year, gradually increasing as the months went on.
2. I’m curious if there’s a specific reason why the water temperature surged more this year compared to previous years. Is there any action we can take to prevent further increases in ocean heat content?
3. This is important to me because rising temperatures could contribute to more severe natural disasters. All communities are growing in heat, and it is not good for us to drift so far from safe, natural temperatures.
4. "As temperatures rise, are you ready for the heat?"

raw_comment:
Because of the recent hurricanes Helene and Milton, we have moved the Taylor Swift graphs ahead by two weeks.  Today’s graph is about the change in temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico over the past twenty years.   You can compare the temperature for the years, but you can also compare the months’ temperature.  Do the Gulf’s temperature cause hurricanes OR do the hurricanes cause the temperatures?  Or, do we not know?  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  If you include a claim, please back it up with evidence that supports your claim.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included this graph, shout outs for some of the catchiest headlines and more.  

You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next graph will be released by Friday, October 25.  The topic – issues most important to swing voters.

raw_comment: It is evident that the Gulf of Mexico's temperatures have risen quickly between 2013 and 2024. August through October have consistently had the warmest temperatures. But those temperatures have reached startling heights in 2024. The highest recorded temperatures were over 80 kj/cm^2. Storms have been able to form more frequently and with even greater force due to this increase in thermal energy. Climate change and global warming are undoubtedly to blame for this. I'm curious how many more years it will take for the southern land mass to dramatically decrease as a result of the increased frequency of storms. Since these storms will eventually move north, this has an impact on my neighborhood. When they do, they will wreak havoc on the northern region.

raw_comment:
From 2013 to 2024, it is clear that the temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico have rapidly increased. The highest temperatures have always been seen from August- October. However, in 2024, those temperatures have risen to staggering heights. The highest temperatures have reached above 80 kj/cm^2. This increase in thermal energy has allowed for storms to form more frequently with even stronger power. This is clearly a result of global warming and climate change. I wonder how many more years it will take for there to be drastically reduced land mass in the south due to this increase in storms. This affects my community because these storms will eventually move their way north. When they do, they will cause mass destruction to the Northern part of the United States. 
Headline: Climate Change In The Gulf of Mexico

How does this relate to your and your community?

While my community at a local level is not affected on a severe level, it’s important to note that some aspects of this graph could be attributed to recent hurricanes, which have affected many people in the U.S.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the graph displays 3 different lines. The red line shows recent temperatures the Gulf of Mexico has had till October 7th, the dotted line shows the average temperature between 2013 to 2023 and the light grey lines show all data from past years. The graph expresses the temperature in kilojoules. This led me to notice that this year (2024) has had the highest temperatures out of all years specifically from June to October. 
2. I wonder if temperatures keep increasing would we have an increase in stronger storms than Milton and Helene? I also wonder why is it that heat affects these hurricanes instead of the cold. 
3. This is related to me and my community because if heat affects all bodies of water and is constantly increasing throughout the years, this would result in greater and stronger storms that can be life-threatening to those living near any body of water in not only the US but the world. 
4. Headline: Hurricanes Milton and Helene have stressed the Gulf of Mexico

raw_comment:
1. I notice that for the most part the temperatures follow the same pattern throughout the years. This is very interesting because the hurricane had an impact on the temperature but now by a lot. For the most part it seems the temperature rises in June and August only to shrink again in October to December.
2. I wonder if the hurricane has much impact on the water temperature. You can see a slight rise this year but I wonder if that was from the hurricane or if it just happened to be a little warmer this year. I would be very interested to see if the hurricane had a significant effect on the water temperature or not.
3. This relates to me and my community as I know many of friends have family in Florida who have to deal with the disaster and destruction the hurricane brought. It is also important to Americans as a whole when one of our states is undergoing such terrible things due to naturally occurring disasters.
4. Milton and Helene are burning the ocean.

1) What do you notice?- The red line indicates 2024, more specifically Oct 7, 2024. The red line has shown us some of the warmest waters in the Gulf of Mexico. We also see the dotted line as the average and the red line is nowhere near that. We also see earlier in the year the gulf was on average then started to warm up past it only coming back to the average twice more in August and July. 4) What’s going on in this graph? - Feel the burn: The Gulf of Mexicos Fiery Temperatures Awaits!

raw_comment:
A Storm is Brewing!
As the hurricane season approaches, I notice the heat rises. Typically around  August through October. I also noticed that the year 2024 is the highest out of all the years. I wonder if this will continue to get worse as time goes on and if this is caused due to climate change. I also wonder if this could be reversed. Although this doesn't relate to me or my community it makes me worry because if this starts to get worse I worry about my family's safety even the safety of other people who aren't family if they live close to the water or if they are in the areas that get affected by these hurricanes.

This suggests that several hurricanes might occur around that time, as the moisture in the air can contribute to hurricane formation.

How does this relate to you and your community?: The graph is relevant to me and my community because it highlights how rising temperatures impact climate change. The heat shifting towards us leads to fluctuations in temperature, which can create conditions for tornadoes that pose serious risks.

raw_comment:
I notice that in 2024 the heat of the Gulf of Mexico has increased quite a bit from previous years. This makes me wonder why the Gulf of Mexico has such a dramatic increase and if there is something that we can do as individuals to normalize the temperature. I also noticed that it just went down during the month of september not only during 2024 but all of the years included this makes me wonder what makes the Gulf cool down during this month. This also is really worrying because we have seen that the more warmth the Gulf has the more reach the hurricanes have on the United States this is no longer a coastal states problem but a US problem. 
This relates to me and my community because  a lot of family members that live in the areas where this has impacted them recently. Not only are they losing their homes but they are also losing their hope of living there because of hurricanes becoming more difficult to control. Is the reason why we have bigger and more aggressive hurricanes caused by the sudden increase in temperature? 
A good Headline for this graph would be " Can you feel the heat off this graph?"

raw_comment: Instantly, what I noticed is that the 2024 heat of the water's surface was originally along the average, but since May has been above that average (except for a time in July).  Before May, the average energy of the water's surface has been typical of the past decade.  However, a lot of years in the past decade also have been way hotter; multiple years have gone past that average, and the only reason that it is an average is because a lot of years have been colder during this time.  Which lines on the graph, and thus years in the past decade, are above the average for the decade and above the average for the decade?  Without this question's answer, we cannot be able to tell an actual trend of the Gulf's temperature, which would be able to confirm or deny another question: Does this evidence help to prove Climate Change?  Or does it prove the unpredictability of the Earth?  In the past, I have considered moving down to Florida because of a college I was potentially interested in.  However, if I did end up going to that college, I would have to worry about the potential for hurricanes which only seems to increase with the increased water surface temperature.  Additionally, even if I stay here with my family and co, hurricanes might make it to Kansas, which would be a nightmare to deal with, especially if they keep increasing in ferocity.  Lastly, for a "catchy" title, "kJ/cm^2: Why THIS Is A Unit To Care For!"

raw_comment:
Warmer waters in the Gulf of Mexico have been taking the United States by storm, literally!

Recently, warmth in the waters of the Gulf of Mexico may be causing worse weather. Recent hurricanes have been ravaging the East Coast. Specifically, hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene did massive damage. But what is causing these damaging storms?

I noticed that the graph shows that this year, the water in the Gulf of Mexico is at an all-time high. This could be because of global warming and melting ice caps. These warmer waters fuel the small tropical storms until they become large hurricanes. These hurricanes cause extensive damage to anything in their path.  

I see that some years had a lower average water temperature than usual. I wonder if those years had different severities of hurricanes or if they were the same. If we had specific information for each year, we could find out.

Hurricanes in the east and what happens to them affect us where we live. We get storms that form from what is left of hurricanes often, and some of them are very severe.  These storms can damage houses and can injure people. It is important that we find out how these storms are affected by the warmer waters and how we can prevent them.

1) What do I notice?

The greatest heat content is in about late August this year, while the lowest is about March. August to October has shown mostly the highest heat contents each year. The higher heat contents of the sea could cause weather phenomena so we have to study all we can to make sure we are prepared.

4) What’s going on in this graph?

Summer Sea Boils! Can You Handle The Heat?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that the ocean heat content per square meter has increased from the previous years and is way higher than the average. I also notice that different parts of the year cause different spikes to happen. Lastly, I see that specifically between the months of August and October, there is normally a spike that causes the ocean heat content to decrease substantially. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder what causes the ocean heat content to increase every year. We notice that every year, the ocean heat content increases. Could this be mainly due to global warming or other factors? Also, does the higher ocean heat content cause more hurricanes to happen?

How does this relate to you and your community?

Ocean heat content plays a large part in the area I am in. I live in the Bay Area, which is really close to the Pacific Ocean. The ocean mainly determines the climate for the surrounding area since it is so large and contains a lot of energy. (kj) This affects my community since a higher ocean temperature would mean the Bay Area would be hotter. This would increase power consumption(Air Conditioning) and also increase the overall temperature of the weather.

raw_comment:
I noticed that even though the Gulf of Mexico ocean temperature always tends to spike in the summer and drop around winter, it seems to have gone significantly higher in this summer of 2024, possibly being affected by global warming. I also noticed that the temperature spiked during August and dropped suddenly in mid-September.

I wonder if the temperature spikes are related to the hurricanes or if the hurricanes are affected by the temperature spikes. We can assume that there is a correlation between the two as there was a spike in mid-September around when Hurricane Helene hit and a sudden drop when Milton hit.

My community in California is not affected by hurricanes, yet the greater America is affected as hurricanes, directly correlated to water temperature in the Gulf of Mexico cause lots of infrastructure damage and humanitarian displacement. If any hurricanes or global warming lead to Florida being completely flooded, other coastal cities like that in California might be the place where Floridians stay.

I notice how the heat appears to peak during summer/fall months, before declining once again. 
I also notice how this pattern repeats annually. The average yearly trends are similar, although not as drastic as this years’. In addition, most individual years followed a similar pattern.

The main red graph line shows the average of all the years in the data set. I wonder if the red line stands for the overall global warming and that is why the line has been much higher for the past couple of years. I wonder if the dot at the beginning of October represents the temperature of the water going back to its regular temperature and transitioning from its elevated state from the previous months. The graph does not impact me directly but it shows how global warming is having an impact on the world's oceans, the ocean temperature does not affect Minnesotans though. Global warming, however, would impact everyone and all of us because global warming is felt by everyone. The catchy title I have created is the tides of temperature and it relates to the temperature in the Gulf of Mexico.

raw_comment: I noticed that the water was significantly higher than the average in the spring/early summer and end of summer/early fall. I am curious what made the water so cold in September one year. I see that the water slowly warms up in the spring and summer and then the temperature drops rapidly in the fall. I wonder what the gap in the graph in June 2024. I am curious if the very high 2024 water temperatures played a role in the intensity of the recent hurricanes because I have seen that hurricanes are more likely to happen with warm waters. I noticed that the graph is slowly getting taller and taller, will this lead to even more and more intense tropical storms/hurricanes in the future? What do all of the breaks in the graph mean? What caused the early temperature spike of a previous year in May? I see this graph having a global impact. If the temperatures continue to rise and the severity of storms increases, many more lives will be destroyed and communities will cease to exist. I see this as a global impact because we all share one world and the temperature is rising everywhere and effecting everyone, in potentially different ways but it is effecting everyone who is on this planet. My catchy headline is 'Hurricanes Are Heating Up".

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I notice that the graph has had previous other data calculated from before the current hurricanes— Helen & Milton— took place. The previously recorded data seemed to be much lower than the present recorded data, which is represented in the color red. The heat content is also much higher during the months of August through October, with a very high and drastic change in heat content.

What do you wonder?
Are these high ocean temperatures safe for the oceanic environment? Did this put any ocean creatures at risk? Does water high temperature ignite hurricanes or any possible disasters?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This overall relates to mine and everyone elses environment. Although we cannot change the heat temperature of the ocean, we can certainly work to make a difference. The current tragic events that have been taking place were possibly caused by climate change and the lack of care we have for our planet and overall environment. If we all manage to work together to change our ways of living, maybe such disasters would not be causing huge changes in oceanic temperature.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the ocean heat content in the Gulf of Mexico during 2024 is much higher than the average from 10 years prior, 2013-2023. The red line for 2024 is significantly above all other average heat contents of other years. The graph only shows the months from February to December. 
2. I wonder if the reason for the chaotic hurricanes has been due to the warmth accumulating in the Gulf of Mexico. I also wonder if the reason the creator of the graph only chose those specific months is because those are the times where heat is more built up in the ocean. 
3. This relates to my community because the hurricanes likely caused by these high accumulations of heat in this part of the ocean have passed by the home countries of the people in my town. Most of the people in my town are from the Caribbean, meaning these hurricanes have been devastating our countries. Cuba, which is my home country and closest to these storms and the Gulf of Mexico's ocean, has been specifically devastated. 
4. It's Getting Hot in Here, Take a Swim!: Gulf of Mexico's Heat Rapidly Increases

raw_comment:
I notice that this year has been way higher in terms of ocean heat content in the gulf of Mexico which shows their waters are heating quickly. This year is substantially above the average of 2013-2023. Between June and August, this year wasn’t that much higher than the average, but we see a huge difference from August to October up until the present day. I also notice more of a variation between the individual years between August and October. Overall, there's less variation in the winter months. 

I wonder why this year, specifically, we have seen such a large difference in the average water temperature. I also wonder why we see the greatest variation from August to October. I wonder if this is from weather patterns or hurricane season. I also wonder why there was a huge jump above the average in June of this year. How do the hurricanes change water temperatures?

This weather pattern really impacts all of us because it demonstrates global warming. This isn’t just happening in the Gulf of Mexico; waters are heating up all around the world. This global warming will impact my local community in terms of weather patterns, environmental conditions, and environmental damage.

Gulf of Mexico on fire: examining water temperature patterns

raw_comment: In a lake, every year the entire body of water cycles itself through. From the cold winter months where the heat sinks to the warm summer days where the cold water sinks. This phenomenon is much like the Atlantic Gulf Stream. During the winter, northern sea ice and decreased temperatures decrease the ocean temperatures, while during summer the warmer Caribbean waters start flowing north. This cycle is, in part, what causes the hurricane season. 1)       I see that the ocean temperature for each month is shown by the red line. Compared to the gray lines that reflect prior years, the red line for this year is higher. The ocean's heat may be rising annually due to global warming, but this year's increase is more rapid than previous ones.

I'm worried about what the weather in the United States will be like in the future. It appears that the weather has been getting worse in every way.
4)         The Gulf of Mexico heats in 2024 in comparison to previous years.

raw_comment:
What stood out to me was how the red line that indicates ocean temperature each month is much higher than the past grey lines. Since the temperature in the Gulf is very high, this could be a direct reason to the amount of dangerous hurricanes this fall. 

This graph sparked some questions and curiosities for me such as: I wonder why the hurricanes this month rapidly intensified over the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico and what factors contributed to the increase? How will this impact the next few months where the temperature will be as high as the lowest temperature during peak hurricane season? Is there a way to fix this?

Relate the graph to your life and community.
In Florida, it is very important to know the conditions of our oceans and where hurricanes can form. Knowing this data can provide necessary information to help us better understand the strength that storms and allow us to better prepare for them. People located near the Gulf may need to prepare if the data in the graph continues to increase. 

Summarize the main idea of the graph with a headline:
Gulf of Mexico: Highest Temperatures to Date!

raw_comment:
We can see a significant temperature increase in August and October in the Gulf of Mexico. Important to note that before that before June we can see also jump in temperature, and then before August the temperature, stays slightly above the norm. It is reasonable to connect the temperature jump, compared to the average, in August and October, to two recent hurricanes.

Still, they do not provide any legitimate proof, even the correlation of how the temperature influences hurricane formation. Thus the question is this connection even true, if so how do they correlate?

I noticed in months with frequent hurricanes the Gulf of Mexico shows hotter temperatures. I noticed this year's line is higher than the rest. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if the hurricanes are affecting the temperature of the water or if the temperature of the water creating hurricanes. I wonder if because hurricane Milton was so bad it was hotter than in other years or was it due to rising global temperatures in general. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

I also am concerned that if this has something to do with global warming this will have negative consequences for our earth as a whole.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the heat of the Gulf of Mexico has dramatically increased over the years, reaching a peak in September and October. 
What do you wonder?

I wonder if this is contributing to the recent hurricanes and tropical storms that have been occurring. What led to this increase in temperature? Will it continue to increase, or will the temperatures drop to where they were previously? What can we do to decrease the temperatures? 

How does this relate to you and your community?
As it does not directly affect me and my community since I live nowhere near the Gulf of Mexico, it affects the people living nearby. These high temperatures can cause problems for the people down south. However, these temperatures are most likely leading to storms, and those effects spread to where I live in Michigan, where we have been experiencing heavy rain and storms. 

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Growing degrees in the Gulf

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I notice that the warmth of the Gulf of Mexico has increased by a significant amount.  This drastic change in temperature is seen specifically in the months of April to June, where the temperature spiked above average, and August to October, where the temperatures were greater than double the average.  By further analyzing this information, I notice that both Hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene were said to have intensified over the increasingly warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico.  I wonder if the devastation of these two hurricanes would have been remarkably lower if the waters had been the average temperature or even below average.  I also wonder if this will impact possible future hurricanes during the fall season in the Gulf of Mexico region and area.  I wonder if the spike of warm waters was caused by the harmful effects of global warming in the world.  The warmth of the body of water is affecting natural disasters, which can further damage communities near the Gulf of Mexico and possibly other regions if global warming continues to warm the oceans.  Global warming and its effects impact me and my community because I have seen firsthand warmer winters and summers than I am previously used to.  My community has witnessed warmer seasons due to global warming, and I wonder if I will witness another warmer winter this year.

raw_comment:
headline: Intensifying Heat in the Gulf of Mexico Powers Strong Hurricanes

The graph measures the warmth of the Gulf of Mexico, specifically—the ocean's heat, over time.  In some parts, I noticed that the red line representing the ocean's heat is higher than the average from 2023-2023. From February to April, the temperatures are pretty average, however May to June there is a significant rise above the average. The ocean heat in October 2024, when the hurricanes are taking place, is much higher compared to previous years (above 80 kj/cm). This makes me wonder what is causing this uprise in heat, one reason potentially being climate change. Also, how does the intense heat create a more powerful hurricane? This graph relates to me and my community because the heat uprising can result in more powerful hurricanes, possibly in my area. Also, more hurricanes in the U.S. means more money is being spent on the clean-up and rebuilding of places hit.

I notice in the graph this year's temperatures have reached unprecedented levels, with some areas nearing 90 degrees Fahrenheit. raw_comment:
Headline: Global Warming Creates Warmth in the Gulf of Mexico 

It's alarming to note that in 2024, the ocean's heat content is projected to surpass the average for previous years, underscoring the urgency of the situation.
I noticed the ocean heat content was similar to the average from February to June. However, the reason why the average ocean content temperature increases from August to October is much more significant. I wonder why there is such a sudden increase in August, whereas the average for previous years was much more stable. This graph is trying to display the consequences of global warming. This year, there has been an increase and a sudden rise in the ocean content temperature, which shows how prominent global warming has become. This graph shows the severity of global warming, which relates to me and my community. This past summer, it was boiling, which was an effect of global warming. This affected me and my community because it was hard to function outside in the heat, and many had to stay inside when it was boiling.

raw_comment:
1) I notice that the ocean heat in the Gulf of Mexico has been shifting, and 2024 is alarming and/or concerning. We observe the graph well enough. The heat in October 2024 is much higher than any of the past ten years (2013-2024). I think that it is very clear that something pivotal has somehow changed this year. What could have changed?

2) I wonder why 2024 is facing this huge spike in ocean heat. Is this without deviation related to climate change or perhaps something else like more hurricanes setting up in the Gulf? I also wonder how this further heat could affect things like the intensity of future storms or even marine life in this area.

3) Even though I live in Perth Amboy, New Jersey (far from the Gulf of Mexico), these changes can still affect me and my community one way or another. More powerful hurricanes and storms can lead to more extreme weather here, including more flooding. Climate change (because of this) can impact our local fishing and waterfront areas, demonstrating how we actually are connected to these changes even though we are located differently.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the chart is showing the average temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico over months in 2024. There is a massive spike in temperature around September, which seems to be the result of Hurricane Helene and Hurricane Milton. This year’s water temperature is marked in red whereas the average temperatures from 2013-2023 are marked with a dotted line. 2024 temperatures in general seem relatively high over all of the months.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how the hurricanes will impact the temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico for the rest of 2024, and the years following. How long will it take for the temperature to level out again? Will the temperatures be higher or lower when the next hurricane hits?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because even though the hurricane doesn’t directly hit us, our weather in Michigan will be impacted as a result of the hurricanes at a later time. This could impact people from Michigan who are planning on traveling to areas impacted by the hurricane for vacation.

raw_comment:
I notice that the level of heat in the Gulf has undergone a massive spike since 2013. It took a nosedive earlier this year, but it went back up with a passion. 
I wonder what climate change has to do with it and if the hurricanes will continue to worsen at the same rate. If not, what is the highest power level of a hurricane that is physically possible?
This impacts my community because I have friends who have relatives in Florida and my grandparents typically like to spend the winter down there. 
Gulf Temperatures Peak As Hurricane Milton Crashes In

Charlye Reiner

This data can provide us important information in regards to the conditions of our oceans as well as our atmosphere, allowing us to better understand the strength that storms may undertake in the future in addition to allowing us to better prepare for them. Finally, If I could give this graph a headline it would be: “Hurricane Bowl; The Gulf’s Territory”

(I’m sure if I thought about it for long enough, I could come up with a better title)

	I notice that the graph very steeply curves up in June, and curves back down in October. I also noticed that the highest it has ever been is October 7th of this year. The line seems to be at its highest point between August and October. 
	I wonder how the heat of the ocean is measured, if so much of it is still unknown to humans. I also wonder if the heat of the ocean has a consistent pattern of going up or if it fluctuates between years. Finally, I wonder why the ocean is so much hotter this year (especially in June) than it’s ever been. 
	This relates to me and my community because this graph is yet another example of global warming, which has an impact on the whole world. If the ocean keeps getting warmer, ice in the colder parts of the world will start to melt and cause flooding. Furthermore, a warmer ocean means more rainfall and hurricanes. 

Headline: Hotter Oceans Help Hurricanes

raw_comment:
I noticed that the temperatures from October 7th, 2024, are almost 20 kilojoules more than those from October 7th, 2013, per square centimeter. This means the temperature has significantly increased across the measured area.
I wonder if either the recent hurricane caused the temperature rise or if global warming did. 
The graph relates to my community because it shows the negative effects of global warming. When one looks at the graph, one sees how much the temperature has risen since 2013, which helps one to acknowledge the Earth’s rising heat. If many people acknowledge this then there’s a slim chance something can be done about this. The warmer temperatures are not subjected to the ocean, the whole Earth is warming up. 
Headline: Heat Waves: How Has Warmth in the Gulf Of Mexico Contributed to Milton and Helene?

What I notice:
I noticed that the average ocean temperature over 2013-2023 is significantly less than the ocean temperature in October 2024. I also noticed that they are measuring the temperature of the Gulf of Mexico. Lastly, I noticed that the temperature increase is related to both Hurricane Milton and Hurricane Helene that hit hard this month.
What I wonder:
I wonder if we can use the information about the temperature of the Gulf of Mexico to predict any future hurricanes. I also wonder if this is the hottest the Gulf of Mexico has been. The graph shows it being the hottest since 2013 but I wonder if years previously if it has been hotter. Finally, I wonder how many more hurricanes are expected to pass through the Gulf of Mexico until hurricane season is over.

raw_comment:
Global Warming: A Threat to the Gulf of Mexico Ecosystem

The Gulf of Mexico is experiencing significant increases in temperature due to a combination of factors, including climate change, ocean currents, and human activities. Rising global temperatures contribute to warmer sea surface temperatures, while alterations in oceanic circulation patterns can exacerbate these effects. Additionally, increased runoff from land, often laden with pollutants, can further elevate water temperatures and disrupt local ecosystems.

raw_comment:
Headline: Interesting factors on the ocean heat content.

I noticed the difference in the ocean content and the way it has gotten bad over the last 10 years. I also noticed how we took a gap year between the hurricane then went back and had the worst one .

My wonder is how do you know about the ocean content and how did you get this type of evidence if the ocean was never fully discovered? And do you think we can use this data to predict the next hurricane?

I would say it relates to my community and this is basically preparing us and it gives us tips for the next hurricane just in case.

raw_comment:
Upon looking at this graph, I notice that the average heat of our oceans (within the defined parameters) seems to have endured its highest levels in the past 11 years.  It looks like the summer months had an incredibly high heat content on average, especially compared to earlier measurements.  I also notice that October (while it still has a much higher heat content than previous years), has undergone a "dip" in heat content compared to the summer of 2024, a trait i presume relates to the changing of the seasons.

I wonder what factors (I presume some sort of human interference) contribute most to the distinguishable rise in heat content in the Gulf of Mexico?  What nation(s) is to blame for these changes, if any nation(s) is to blame in the first place?  Why exactly are the temperatures so much more different than previous years?  Could these enormous differentiations be attributed to the implementation of new equipment?

My immediate community and I are located far away from the Gulf of Mexico, so this heat content change is not too problematic for anything like industry or farming.  That being said, with that large of a body of water undergoing these changes, the weather patterns that form from said body of water may most definitely affect my community, in the form of changes in the winter climate (possibly less snow), and small implications with agriculture.  I'm not too worried.

raw_comment:
- I noticed that 2024's water heat increase follows a similar pattern to other years, but is elevated by several kjs in a couple places. This is undoubtedly due to the two hurricanes we've experienced in the past year, but I'm not sure why extreme weather conditions would elevate the temperatures.
- I wonder what the heat index of the gulf of Mexico was like in years past, before 2013. Is this the hottest the ocean water has been in the gulf? Has the water temperature increased due to hurricanes before?
- I don't know a lot about the gulf of Mexico, but my grandma lives in a part of Florida that was hit hard by Milton. Luckily, nothing too bad happened, but her street's been out of power since the hurricane hit. It's important to stay well informed on natural disasters, even tangentially. 
- Milton and Helene raise the gulf of Mexico to temperatures not seen for more than a decade.

raw_comment:
I noticed that on average, over the years, there is a notable increase in the heat within the Gulf of Mexico. However, in 2024, the trend was abundantly higher compared to other years. This may explain why there were many hurricanes such as Hurricane Helene and Hurricane Milton almost back to back.

I wonder what makes hurricanes different from cyclones or typhoons? How did one come up with the cut-off for wind speed for the categories of a hurricane? I also wonder if it is possible that one day in the future with the sea levels rising, hurricanes could go into the midlands of America and how that would affect the coastlines.

It relates to the community and me because knowing of the increase in heat can help us further prepare for disasters such as hurricanes in the upcoming years. Knowing that there is a “hurricane season” can help us prepare and ensure we are safe for when hurricanes come again. 

“In the Heat of It: The Rise of Scorching Heat Content since 2013 in the Gulf of Mexico Continues to Contribute to the Deadly Hurricanes of Today”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the graph shows the average amount of thermal energy stored from the sea surface down through the ocean depths. In 2024, however, the average is a lot higher. It was rapidly increasing. Warmer water allows storms to build up and get more intense. This is not good because of the hurricanes continuing to grow.


What do you wonder?
I wonder why warm water makes storms strengthen. I wonder what caused some of the averages to be really low. What years compare with this year the best? Why does August and October have such a big spike in temperature, but in between June and August doesn’t?


How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because this is an effect of the hurricanes which are happening around Florida. It is important to stay updated about what is happening so that people can stay safe. 


Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Heating Up Hurricane Milton and Helene; How Hot Will the Gulf of Mexico Get?
